ann_82.text: Calls to customer service add to the predicted chance from about 3 calls upwards (between 2 and 5 calls for different customers), in an uneven way across customers: going from 0 to 4 calls moves a typical customer from about 4% to about 12% (on the training data only).
A higher daytime charge lowers it steadily up to about $25.13 (between $25.13 and $31.31 for different customers), then no further: from $15.49 to $59.76, about 12% to 4% (on the training data only).

This part acts on 1348 of 4000 customers (202 of them left), and for a typical one (with two customer-service calls and about 132 daytime minutes costing about $22) it raises the predicted chance only slightly, from about 2% to about 3%.

For a typical customer both effects are slight: the daytime charge lowers it steadily up to that point, then no further, and going from 0 to 3 calls raises it in an uneven way; being in Michigan, Nebraska or New Jersey also lowers it only slightly (on the training data only).

ann_83.text: In this part, more daytime minutes clearly lower the predicted chance for a typical customer in an uneven way, from about 56% at 112 minutes to about 1% at 249 minutes, and a higher evening charge clearly lowers it, also in an uneven way, from about 20% at $11.76 to about 1% at $22.57.
A voice-mail plan clearly raises it here, from about 4% to about 18%.

The fall with daytime minutes happens unevenly across customers, and it is clearly stronger for customers with a voice-mail plan (about 18% to below 1%) and for those with an evening charge at or below about $17 (about 49% to below 1%).
An international plan and customer-service calls change it only slightly here, the calls in an uneven way (on the training data only).

ann_84.text: More daytime minutes raise the predicted chance only slightly here, steadily up to about 160 minutes, then no further (on the training data only).
This part acts on 1429 of 4000 customers, and 170 of them left.

ann_85.text: Area codes 408 and 510 and being in Missouri, Massachusetts, New York, Florida, Kentucky, Michigan, Texas, Oklahoma or Ohio change the predicted chance only slightly (on the training data only).
Being in Ohio changes it only slightly, and only for area code 408.

ann_86.text: Across the whole model, a higher daytime charge clearly raises the predicted chance for a typical customer, slowly at first, then faster, from below 1% at $19 to about 61% at $42, while more daytime minutes clearly lower it in an uneven way, from about 41% at 112 minutes to about 1% at 249 minutes.
An international plan clearly raises it from about 4% to about 35%.
Being in California (about 12%), Washington (about 11%) or New Jersey (about 9%) raises it (on the training data only).

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted chance only slightly (on the training data only): more evening minutes, a higher night-time or international charge, more voice-mail messages and a longer account each raise it steadily; each extra international call lowers it by about the same amount; and area code and the other states change it a little, with Hawaii, Vermont and Colorado lowest at about 1% or below.
A voice-mail plan and going from 0 to 3 customer-service calls change it only slightly, the calls in an uneven way.
It ignores the number of daytime, evening and night-time calls, total international minutes and total night-time minutes.

With 0-2 calls it is a plain low-day-charge hinge (z < -0.76; about +1.5 logit at z < -1.5). With 4+ calls it fires across a wider day range: mean +4.35 logit at day z<-1.5 and +2.97 at -1.5..-0.5, where churn is 100% (16 rows) and 89% (76 rows), against 3-7% for 0-3 calls. Evidence (train, n=4000): closed form; sensitivity is largest for dayCharge (0.23) and state:29 (0.20), then csc (0.11); linearising this child alone costs 0.007 AUC, restoring it alone onto the fully linearised model adds +0.047. Rare-state gates: state:29 (72 rows) switches the unit off (-1.8 logit on 10 rows, 1 churner); state:31 (-2.8 on 2 rows) and state:22 similar.
ann_82.proposed: Customer-service calls from about 3 upwards raise the predicted chance, and a higher daytime charge lowers it steadily up to about $25.13, then no further.

ann_83.original: Usage hinge plus a second service-call x low-usage path. With 7068 = 0 the relays are constant (7561=1.31, 12924=2.68, 9009=4.43+0.83*vmp), so 4496 = relu(1.79 - 2.01*dayMin - 1.08*eveCharge + 0.56*voiceMailPlan), output +1.31. It cancels the direct day (+2.83 dayCharge +0.27 dayMin) and eve (+0.95 eveCharge +0.42 eveMin) slopes below high usage: the net day slope is about +0.5/z below z~0.9 and +3.1/z above, so churn rises steeply only for heavy day+eve users (33% churn at day z 1-2, 72% at z>2, vs 8-12% below). A voice-mail plan shifts the hinge (+1.24 logit at low usage, offsetting part of the -2.8 direct edge). Branch: 10224 -> 10574 -> 21697 rises with day minutes and an international plan; 7068 = relu(0.467*csc - 1.18*21697 - 0.359) opens only at 3+ calls with low day usage and no international plan (306 rows) and feeds 4496 through the relays with gain ~4.2 (about +5.5 logit per unit of 7068): +8.6 mean contribution at 4+ calls and day z -1.5..-0.5 vs +4.7 at 0-2 calls. 10574 and 21697 also reach the output directly with tiny weights (-0.04, -0.02). Evidence (train): closed form; sensitivity of 4496 dominated by dayMin (1.69) and eveCharge (0.85). ann_84.original: 20486 = relu(-2.03*dayMin - 0.758), output -0.14: a small correction lowering churn logit for very low day minutes (z < -0.37), mean -0.57 logit at z < -2, -0.29 at -2..-1. Usage + csc gate together recover 0.9165.

summary.text: For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, with no international or voice-mail plan, one call to customer service and median usage, such as about 180 daytime minutes), the predicted chance that a customer leaves is about 4%, and having an international plan clearly raises it to about 35%.

A higher daytime charge clearly raises it, slowly at first, then faster, from below 1% at $19 to about 61% at $42, while more daytime minutes, which carry the same information, clearly lower it in an uneven way, from about 41% at 112 minutes to about 1% at 249 minutes.

Customers in California (about 12%), Washington (about 11%) and New Jersey (about 9%) get a higher predicted chance than customers in West Virginia (on the training data only).
A voice-mail plan lowers it only slightly across the whole model, and going from 0 to 3 customer-service calls changes it only slightly, in an uneven way.
The model ignores the number of daytime, evening and night-time calls, total international minutes and total night-time minutes.
